items.stem: The provision allowing each German state to make alliances with foreign powers most directly reflects which of the following developments in the Holy Roman Empire after 1648?

options.text: The empire became a loose association of largely self-governing states with a weak emperor.
options.label: key
options.why: The treaty confirmed the states' territorial rights and their right to make foreign alliances. In practice this left the emperor with little real power over the princes, and the empire became a decentralized collection of nearly sovereign states.

options.text: The emperor gained authority over the foreign policies of all German princes, bishops, and free cities.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The excerpt does the opposite. It gives the states, not the emperor, the right to make alliances with foreign powers.

options.text: The German states were united into a single nation-state under the leadership of the Prussian monarchy.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: German unification under Prussian leadership happened in 1871, more than two centuries after Westphalia.

options.text: Each German state gained full independence and ended all legal obligations to the emperor and the empire.
options.label: overstated
options.why: The excerpt keeps the oath binding every state to the emperor and the empire, and it bans alliances against them. The states' freedom was large but not unlimited.

facts: The Peace of Westphalia (1648) confirmed the territorial rights of the German princes and their right to make alliances with foreign powers.
After 1648 the Holy Roman Empire was highly decentralized, and the emperor had limited authority over the member states.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The clause giving each state a perpetual right to make alliances with 'Strangers' shows how far authority had shifted from the emperor to the states.
design.evidence_quote: it shall be free perpetually to each of the States of the Empire, to make Alliances with Strangers for their Preservation and Safety

items.stem: The treaty's stated aim "to prevent for the future any Differences arising in the Politick State" is best explained by which of the following historical situations?

options.text: Imperial attempts to curb the princes' powers had helped start and prolong a destructive war.
options.label: key
options.why: Habsburg efforts to enforce imperial and Catholic authority, such as the Edict of Restitution of 1629, set off resistance from the princes and helped drag out the Thirty Years' War. Guaranteeing the states' rights was meant to keep such conflicts from starting again.

options.text: German princes had united behind the emperor to restore Catholic uniformity across the empire.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The princes were divided by religion, and many fought the emperor. The settlement protected princely rights instead of restoring Catholic uniformity.

options.text: Peasant revolts inspired by Luther's teachings had overthrown many princes in the German lands during the war.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The German Peasants' War took place in 1524 to 1525 and was put down by the princes. It was not part of the situation behind the 1648 settlement.

options.text: A civil war between Parliament and the king had ended with the execution of the English monarch Charles I.
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: This is English history, and Charles I was executed in January 1649, after the treaty. It has nothing to do with disputes inside the Holy Roman Empire.

facts: The Thirty Years' War (1618-1648) began with a Bohemian Protestant revolt against Habsburg authority.
Emperor Ferdinand II's Edict of Restitution (1629) tried to restore church lands to Catholic control and deepened Protestant resistance.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt opens with its purpose, preventing future disputes in the political order, and then guarantees the states' rights against molestation 'by any whomsoever,' which points to past interference with those rights.
design.evidence_quote: that they never can or ought to be molested therein by any whomsoever upon any manner of pretence

items.stem: The limits on imperial authority confirmed in the excerpt most directly contributed to which of the following developments in central Europe between 1648 and 1740?

options.text: Brandenburg-Prussia rose as a strong state with a large standing army.
options.label: key
options.why: Because they were free of effective imperial control, ambitious princes could build their own power. Frederick William, the Great Elector, and his successors turned Brandenburg-Prussia into a centralized, militarized state.

options.text: A national parliament met in Frankfurt to write a constitution for a united Germany.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Frankfurt Parliament met in 1848 and 1849, well outside the period named in the question.

options.text: Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes and expelled many Huguenots from his French kingdom.
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The revocation of 1685 was a French religious policy. It was not a result of the limits Westphalia placed on the emperor.

options.text: The Habsburg emperors imposed a centralized bureaucracy and uniform laws on all the German princes.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Westphalia kept the emperors from centralizing control over the princes. The Habsburgs instead built up their power in their own hereditary lands.

facts: Frederick William, the Great Elector (r. 1640-1688), built a standing army and a centralized administration in Brandenburg-Prussia.
Frederick William I of Prussia (r. 1713-1740) greatly expanded the Prussian army.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt confirms each state's 'free exercise of Territorial Right' and its freedom to make alliances, which allowed individual princes to build up their own states.
design.evidence_quote: free exercise of Territorial Right, as well Ecclesiastick, as Politick Lordships, Regales

items.stem: EXTRA. Which of the following best describes the excerpt's position on alliances between the German states and foreign powers?

options.text: They were allowed for a state's security but not if aimed at the emperor or empire.
options.label: key
options.why: The excerpt allows alliances 'for their Preservation and Safety' but adds a condition: they must not be against the emperor, the empire, the public peace or the treaty.

options.text: They were allowed for any purpose, including war against the emperor, if a state judged it necessary.
options.label: overstated
options.why: The excerpt explicitly bans alliances against the emperor and the empire.

options.text: They were allowed only after the emperor and the Imperial Diet had approved each treaty in advance.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt calls the right 'free perpetually' and says nothing about any approval process.

options.text: They were forbidden so that the empire could conduct a single foreign policy toward France and Sweden.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The excerpt allows such alliances. It does not forbid them.

facts: The Peace of Westphalia (1648) allowed the imperial states to make alliances with foreign powers as long as they were not directed against the emperor or the empire.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The proviso clause sets the limits on the states' right of alliance.
design.evidence_quote: provided, nevertheless, such Alliances be not against the Emperor, and the Empire, nor against the Publick Peace, and this Treaty

items.stem: EXTRA. The provisions in the excerpt are best understood in the context of which broader development in seventeenth-century European diplomacy?

options.text: A system of sovereign states in which powers like France sought to check Habsburg dominance.
options.label: key
options.why: Catholic France and Lutheran Sweden fought the Habsburgs for reasons of state, and both were parties to the settlement. A weak, divided empire whose states could ally with outsiders fit a balance-of-power system among sovereign states.

options.text: A revival of papal authority to settle disputes among Catholic and Protestant rulers in Europe.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Pope Innocent X condemned the Westphalian settlement. The treaties were negotiated by states, and the papacy's political role shrank.

options.text: The spread of Enlightenment arguments that legitimate governments rest on the consent of the governed.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Consent-based political theory developed later, with Locke in 1689 and the eighteenth-century Enlightenment. The excerpt is about princely rights, not popular consent.

options.text: The growth of Dutch commercial power based on overseas trade, banking, and a large merchant fleet.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Dutch commerce did flourish in this period, but it does not explain a treaty clause about the territorial and alliance rights of German princes.

facts: Catholic France under Cardinal Richelieu entered the Thirty Years' War against the Habsburgs in 1635, and France backed Protestant Sweden.
Pope Innocent X issued a condemnation of the Peace of Westphalia in 1648.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line names Sweden as a party to the treaty, and the excerpt lets the German states ally with foreign powers. Both point to a diplomacy of competing sovereign states that checked Habsburg power.
design.evidence_quote: to make Alliances with Strangers for their Preservation and Safety

items.stem: Which of the following best describes a difference between the main purposes of Source A and Source B?

options.text: Source A pledges joint military action against a named rival, while Source B settles competing colonial claims in North Africa.
options.label: key
options.why: Source A binds both empires to fight Russia with their whole war strength, while Source B's public articles trade British freedom of action in Egypt for French freedom of action in Morocco and contain no military pledge.

options.text: Source A divides overseas spheres of influence between two empires, while Source B pledges full military aid if either signer is attacked by Germany.
options.label: reversal
options.why: This swaps the two documents. Source A is the military pact, and Source B's public text divides spheres of influence and does not mention Germany.

options.text: Both sources create binding military alliances that require the signers to go to war together against any power that attacks either one of them.
options.label: overstated
options.why: Only Source A requires joint war, and even it limits that duty to Russia or Russian-backed attacks. Source B contains no military obligation.

options.text: Source A aims to revise borders drawn at the Congress of Vienna, while Source B aims to end British rule and restore Ottoman authority in Egypt.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Neither text supports this. Source A is defensive and says nothing about the Vienna borders, and in Source B Britain declares it will not change Egypt's status, which leaves its own position there intact.

facts: The Dual Alliance of 1879 was a defensive military alliance between Germany and Austria-Hungary aimed at Russia.
The Entente Cordiale of 1904 settled colonial disputes between Britain and France, chiefly over Egypt and Morocco.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Source A's Article 1 commits both empires to war against Russia; Source B's public articles deal only with the status of Egypt and Morocco.
design.evidence_quote: bound to come to the assistance one of the other with the whole war strength of their Empires

items.stem: Which of the following contexts most directly shaped the focus on Russia in Source A?

options.text: Russian resentment after the Congress of Berlin in 1878 cut back Russian gains in the Balkans
options.label: key
options.why: The Congress of Berlin revised the Treaty of San Stefano and reduced Russia's gains from its war with the Ottomans. Russia blamed Germany and Austria-Hungary, so Bismarck turned to an alliance with Vienna aimed at Russia.

options.text: Russian weakness after its defeat by Japan in 1905, which encouraged the Central Powers to plan an attack eastward
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Russo-Japanese War ended in 1905, twenty-six years after this treaty, and the treaty is defensive, not a plan for attack.

options.text: Fear in Vienna and Berlin of liberal and nationalist uprisings like those that spread across central Europe in 1848
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The revolutions of 1848 came three decades earlier, and the treaty deals with an attack by a foreign power, not with internal revolt.

options.text: Anglo-French victory over Russia in the Crimean War of 1853 to 1856, which left Russia eager to revise the peace terms
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Crimean War came more than two decades before 1879. The more recent Balkan crisis of 1877-1878 and the Congress of Berlin shaped the treaty's focus on Russia.

facts: The Congress of Berlin (1878) revised the Treaty of San Stefano and reduced Russian gains in the Balkans.
Russian anger at Germany and Austria-Hungary after 1878 helped lead to the Dual Alliance of 1879.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Source A names Russia as the expected attacker in both articles, which points to the Russian grievances following the 1878 Congress of Berlin.
design.evidence_quote: one of the two Empires be attacked by Russia

items.stem: In the way it handles rivalry between European powers, Source B most closely resembles which earlier development?

options.text: The Berlin Conference of 1884 to 1885, where European powers set rules for claims in Africa
options.label: key
options.why: Like the Berlin Conference, the 1904 agreement settled imperial rivalry in Africa through negotiation, with European governments deciding the political future of African lands without consulting their peoples.

options.text: The Treaty of Frankfurt of 1871, in which a defeated France ceded Alsace and part of Lorraine to the new German Empire
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Treaty of Frankfurt was a peace imposed on France after military defeat and concerned European territory. Source B is a mutual bargain over spheres of influence in Africa.

options.text: The Holy Alliance of 1815, in which the monarchs of Russia, Austria, and Prussia pledged to uphold Christian principles in governing
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Holy Alliance was a statement of conservative monarchical principles and had nothing to do with dividing colonial influence.

options.text: The Carlsbad Decrees of 1819, which let Metternich impose censorship and police surveillance on universities across the German Confederation
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Carlsbad Decrees were real, but they were domestic repression inside the German Confederation, not diplomacy between rival powers over overseas territory.

facts: The Berlin Conference of 1884-1885 set rules among European powers for claiming African territory.
The Entente Cordiale of 1904 traded British predominance in Egypt for French predominance in Morocco.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Source B shows Britain and France deciding the status of Egypt and Morocco between themselves, which follows the pattern of negotiated European partition of Africa.
design.evidence_quote: it appertains to France... to preserve order in that country

items.stem: Germany's reaction to the British recognition of French interests in Morocco in Source B most directly contributed to which development?

options.text: The First Moroccan Crisis, settled at the Algeciras Conference of 1906
options.label: key
options.why: In 1905 Germany challenged the French position in Morocco, starting with Wilhelm II's visit to Tangier. At the Algeciras Conference of 1906 Britain backed France, and the entente grew stronger instead of breaking apart.

options.text: The Fashoda Crisis, in which British and French forces confronted each other on the upper Nile in Sudan
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Fashoda Crisis happened in 1898, before the 1904 agreement. It was part of the rivalry the Entente later settled, not a German reaction to it.

options.text: The Bosnian Crisis, in which Austria-Hungary annexed Bosnia-Herzegovina over strong objections from Serbia and Russia
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Bosnian Crisis of 1908 was a Balkan dispute among Austria-Hungary, Serbia and Russia and had nothing to do with Morocco.

options.text: The South African War, in which Britain fought the Boer republics of the Transvaal and Orange Free State
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The South African War (1899-1902) ended before the 1904 agreement and was not caused by German policy toward Morocco.

facts: Wilhelm II's visit to Tangier in 1905 set off the First Moroccan Crisis.
The Algeciras Conference of 1906 largely upheld France's position in Morocco, with British support.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Source B's article on Morocco recognizes France's right to act there, the arrangement Germany challenged in 1905.
design.evidence_quote: to provide assistance for the purpose of all administrative, economic, financial , and military reforms which it may require

items.stem: Article 2 of Source A was most likely written to address which concern of German leaders in 1879?

options.text: A two-front war in which Russia backed a French attack on Germany
options.label: key
options.why: Article 2 brings in full Austrian aid if another power attacks with Russian support. After 1871 Bismarck feared that a France seeking revenge might join with Russia and force Germany to fight on two fronts.

options.text: British naval expansion threatening the overseas colonies that Germany had acquired in Africa and the Pacific
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Germany did not acquire colonies until 1884, and the Anglo-German naval rivalry came after 1898, so neither shaped a treaty of 1879.

options.text: Polish nationalist uprisings in Prussian Poland that might spread to the Polish lands of Galicia
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Article 2 covers an attack by another Power, which is war between states, not an uprising inside either empire.

options.text: Ottoman efforts to reconquer Serbia and Romania, whose independence had just been recognized by the great powers
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Serbia and Romania were recognized in 1878, but the Ottomans were not trying to reconquer them, and an Ottoman attack on Germany was not a real German worry.

facts: France lost Alsace-Lorraine to Germany in 1871, and many French people wanted it back.
Bismarck's diplomacy after 1871 aimed to isolate France and avoid a two-front war.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Article 2 brings full mutual aid into force when another power attacks with Russian support, which matches the German fear of a combined attack by France and Russia.
design.evidence_quote: Should, however, the attacking party in such a case be supported by Russia
